variants_and_conflicts.description: Pargiter main text Aruṇākṣa; its footnote gives Bombay Aruṇākhya. SanskritDocuments DM 11.52 reads Aruṇākhya, meaning named Aruṇa.
Wisdomlib index prose labels DM as chapters 82–92; actual linked chapter heading and narrative boundaries are 81–93. Catalogue uses linked headings.
DM9.30 calls Niśumbha ditija; record textual Diti-descendant descriptor, not an independently narrated biological mother–son genealogy.
Wisdomlib Pargiter display has corrupted rain/failure text and says heavy rain in the nourishment sentence; Sanskrit DM 11.46–48 explicitly says drought and nourishment until rain.
Sanskrit DM 11.50 explicitly announces Durgādevī after Durgama’s killing; the displayed Pargiter paragraph omits the name-sentence.
Pargiter canto 83 footnote 2 reports Bombay additions killing Kāla, Ugradarśana and Asiloman. These are footnote-attested variants, excluded from main event order pending edition inspection.
Pargiter’s killing sentence says heads and buttocks; Sanskrit has jaghane. Conventional thigh-position is not imposed until another reliable witness is inspected.
Pārvatī becoming Kālikā in ch5 and Kālī emanating from Ambikā in ch7 are separate source-scoped manifestation nodes; sameness not established by those scenes alone.
Pargiter interprets Kolāvidhvaṃsin as non-destroyers of Kolas; other common retellings translate destroyers. No etymological conclusion imposed.
Pargiter has Mauryas; SanskritDocuments DM 8.6 has Maurvas. Manuscript/print collation needed before standardizing the group-name.
Pargiter ch10 translates absorption into breasts; Sanskrit 10.6 says tanau, body. Graph records only absorption into Devī.
Ch8 emits Caṇḍikā’s Śakti named Śivadūtī; Pargiter ch9 note identifies Śivadūtī with Caṇḍikā. Main graph retains emanation, avoids silently collapsing entities.
Pargiter adopts Ugradarśana as a name from Bombay reading; SanskritDocuments DM 2.43–44 has a participle and no such proper name.

manuscript.aftermath: Madhu and Kaitabha are defeated under the condition they themselves state. Brahma is no longer under their immediate threat, and the bounded episode closes without claiming that the cosmic waters recede or adding events beyond the locked arc.
manuscript.audience: Family read-aloud and independent readers around age ten and above; exact age band requires independent editorial confirmation.

beats.summary: Medhas distinguishes eternal Devi from her purposeful appearances; at cosmic dissolution Vishnu sleeps on Shesha while Madhu and Kaitabha arise from his ear-region and threaten lotus-seated Brahma.
Brahma addresses Yoganidra in an attributed hymn and asks her to delude the demons and awaken Vishnu.
Yoganidra withdraws from the source-named places in Vishnu, appears before Brahma, and enables his awakening; after five thousand years of combat, the deluded demons offer Vishnu a boon.
Vishnu requests that both demons die by his hand, accepts their unflooded-earth condition, and defeats them with his discus without specifying the disputed bodily locus.
A clearly labeled modern editorial reflection invites family discussion without presenting its interpretation as scripture.

chapters.text:
Sage Medhas began with a distinction.

“The Goddess is eternal,” he said. “When the sacred account speaks of her appearing, it tells of the forms by which she becomes known for divine purposes.”

Then his story moved beyond kingdoms, roads and remembered seasons, to the dissolution of a world.

Water stretched through the vastness. No shore divided one direction from another. There was no field to cross, no mountain path to climb, no city lamp to mark a home. The flood of dissolution held the scene in a silence deeper than ordinary night.

Upon Shesha rested Vishnu.

He was not keeping the light sleep of a traveller who might wake at the snap of a twig. Yoganidra, the divine power of cosmic sleep, held him in profound stillness. His breathing alone gave measure to the immeasurable quiet.

From him rose a lotus, and upon that lotus sat Brahma.

The flower stood above the waters like the single open eye of a world not yet remade. Brahma had no ground beneath him—only the lotus, Vishnu below, and the unbroken flood beyond.

Vishnu slept.

The waters waited.

And in that stillness, danger appeared.
chapters.title: The Sleep Beyond the World

chapters.text:
From the region of Vishnu’s ears arose two Asuras: Madhu and Kaitabha.

They entered the story already powerful, moving through the waters of dissolution toward the lotus where Brahma sat.

Their purpose was plain. They threatened to kill him.

Brahma looked from the approaching figures to Vishnu. The preserver still rested upon Shesha, held in the depth of Yoganidra. No call from the lotus had yet broken that sleep.

Madhu and Kaitabha came nearer.

There was nowhere for Brahma to flee. Around the lotus lay the same endless flood. Below it slept the one who could face the threat. Yet the sleep upon Vishnu was itself divine power, not an ordinary weariness that Brahma could simply shake away.

The danger and the answer stood almost together: the threatening Asuras upon the waters, Vishnu beneath the lotus, and the power of sleep holding him still.

Brahma did not address the sleepers with a hurried shout. He turned his praise toward Yoganidra herself.

The silence at the end of the world became a place of invocation.
chapters.title: The Danger at the Lotus

chapters.text:
Brahma gathered his attention and praised the Goddess who held Vishnu in sleep.

“You are the sacred utterance by which offerings are made,” he said. “You are the power by which creation arises, by which it is preserved, and by which it is drawn again into dissolution. You are knowledge, and you are the great illusion that can veil knowledge. You are nature, nourishment and peace. You are also power armed against danger.”

Madhu and Kaitabha continued their approach.

Brahma’s praise became a direct appeal.

“Great Goddess, delude these two Asuras. Withdraw your sleep from Vishnu and awaken him, so that their threat may be ended.”

The lotus did not move away from danger. The waters did not open a road of escape. Nothing in the scene became smaller or safer.

But the invocation had found the power to whom it was addressed.

The change began within the stillness of Vishnu himself.
chapters.title: Brahma’s Invocation

chapters.text:
Yoganidra withdrew from Vishnu’s eyes, mouth and nose; from his arms, heart and breast.

The power that had held Vishnu in cosmic sleep now appeared before Brahma.

For one suspended moment, the whole scene had changed without the waters changing at all. Brahma remained upon the lotus. Madhu and Kaitabha remained near. Shesha still bore Vishnu above the flood.

Yet sleep no longer enclosed him.

Vishnu’s eyes opened.

Stillness gave way to attention. Rest gave way to readiness. He saw Brahma upon the lotus and the two Asuras who had come to destroy him.

Vishnu rose to meet Madhu and Kaitabha.

No army marched into the waters. No ranks gathered behind him. Vishnu met the two Asuras with his arms, and the combat closed around them.

The two Asuras turned from the lotus to face him.

Brahma’s danger had not vanished; it had become a confrontation. Yoganidra had answered the invocation by withdrawing, appearing before Brahma, and opening the way for Vishnu to wake.

Now the long struggle began.
chapters.title: When Sleep Stood Apart

chapters.text:
Vishnu grappled with Madhu and Kaitabha upon the cosmic waters.

A hold was made and broken. One Asura drove forward; Vishnu checked him. The other closed from the side; Vishnu turned to meet him. Again they joined, separated and returned.

Years passed, yet the struggle did not end.

Hundreds became thousands.

For five thousand years, Vishnu fought the two Asuras with his arms.

The story’s measure of time is immense, but its problem is easy to understand: strength met strength, and still the danger remained. Whenever one attacker was forced back, the other pressed in. Whenever both were driven away, they returned to the struggle.

Then Yoganidra’s power brought the reversal Brahma had requested.

Madhu and Kaitabha became deluded. Intoxicated with their own strength, they no longer saw the contest clearly. They had fought Vishnu for five thousand years, and pride made them speak as if the advantage were theirs to give.

Madhu drew back.

“Ask a boon of us,” he said.

Kaitabha stood beside him. “Yes. Choose what we shall give.”

After an age of combat, the strangest moment in the battle was not another blow. It was the offer made by the two who had come as enemies.

They had become the boon-givers.

Vishnu answered them.
chapters.title: Five Thousand Years

chapters.text:
“Then let the boon be this,” Vishnu said. “Let both of you be overcome by me.”

The words changed the shape of the contest.

Madhu and Kaitabha had offered the boon jointly. Vishnu had not asked them for land, treasure or long life. He had asked for the one outcome their pride had not expected to grant: their own defeat at his hands.

Across the scene lay only the flood of dissolution.

Madhu answered, “Only where earth is not flooded.”

Kaitabha added, “On that condition, we grant it.”

It was a condition attached by both demons to the boon they had offered.

Vishnu replied, “I accept.”

The combat had lasted five thousand years. The exchange took only a few words. Yet those words did what force alone had not done: they fixed a condition under which the struggle could end.

The waters were still everywhere around them.

Vishnu met the condition.
chapters.title: The Boon Turned Back

chapters.text:
The place of their defeat met the demons’ condition: the earth there was not under the flood.

Vishnu raised his discus. Its swift circle ended the contest, and Madhu and Kaitabha could no longer threaten the lotus.

Brahma was safe. Vishnu stood awake above the cosmic waters. Yoganidra’s withdrawal had made his awakening possible, and her power had turned the demons’ pride toward the boon that ended them.

Sage Medhas let the struggle come to rest.

The danger at the lotus was over.
chapters.title: Where the Earth Was Not Flooded

chapters.text:
This is a modern editorial reflection, not a quotation from scripture.

Sleep, sustained strength and the boon condition each change the story in a different way: Yoganidra’s withdrawal makes awakening possible, Vishnu endures the long struggle, and the demons’ own condition opens the way to its end.

For family conversation: When a problem will not yield to force, what condition might be holding it in place? What can change when that condition is understood?
chapters.title: Editorial Reflection — A Thought for Families

manuscript.editorial_reflection: Modern editorial reflection, not a source quotation: sleep, sustained strength and the boon condition each change the story differently. Families are invited to ask what condition may be holding a difficult problem in place, and what can change when that condition is understood.
manuscript.ending: Vishnu meets the demons’ unflooded-earth condition and kills Madhu and Kaitabha with his discus. Brahma’s immediate danger ends, Vishnu remains awake, Yoganidra’s role is accounted for, and Medhas’s bounded primordial episode closes before the separately labeled editorial reflection.
manuscript.opening: Sage Medhas distinguishes the eternal Goddess from her purposeful manifestations, then carries the listener into the world-dissolving flood where Vishnu sleeps on Shesha beneath the power of Yoganidra and danger approaches lotus-seated Brahma.
manuscript.source_note: This private editorial draft is fresh original English prose based only on the locked paraphrases and locators for Devi Mahatmya 1 in dm-event-004 through dm-event-007. Brahma’s cosmic and theological descriptions are presented as his attributed hymn-praise, not as independent project certification. All dialogue is non-verbatim adaptation. The five-thousand-year combat, joint boon offer by Madhu and Kaitabha, Vishnu’s requested boon, the unflooded-earth condition and the discus defeat remain in source order. No demon genealogy, earlier ascetic or invulnerability boon, outside boon-giver, divine motive or sacred quotation has been added. Because the bounded English and Sanskrit witnesses leave the final bodily locus unresolved, the manuscript states only that the water condition is met and omits any thigh, lap, buttocks or other precise locus. The DM08 manuscript was consulted only as a literary-quality benchmark and was neither copied nor treated as evidence. This clearance permits only a private manuscript draft; illustration, PDF production, publication, public sharing and distribution remain blocked.
